## How to Choose an E-commerce Logistics Partner in India

To choose an ecommerce logistics partner in India, compare serviceability, total shipping cost, delivery performance, COD handling, RTO processes, integrations and support rather than selecting only the lowest shipping rate. The right logistics partner should fit your product, order volume, customer locations and cash flow, whether you run a small D2C brand, marketplace store or larger fulfilment operation.

A logistics partner is not simply a courier company. It may provide courier aggregation, pickup, warehousing, inventory management, order processing, packaging, return handling, COD reconciliation and delivery reporting. Some businesses need only shipping software and carrier access. Others need D2C fulfilment from a warehouse.

The decision affects customer experience and margins directly. A delayed parcel, failed COD delivery or poorly managed return can cost more than the original freight charge. Before signing up, understand what you are buying, how charges are calculated and what happens when an order does not move as expected.

## Start With Your Shipping Requirements

Before comparing providers, document your current or expected order profile. A partner that works well for a Pune-based cosmetics brand may not suit a furniture seller, a school merchandise store or a pan-India apparel business.

### Product category and package characteristics

Begin with the products you sell. Write down:

- Average product value
- Average packed weight
- Package dimensions
- Fragile or liquid contents
- Perishable or temperature-sensitive goods
- Battery-powered or restricted items
- Typical number of items per order
- Packaging material required
- Whether the product can be shipped in a polybag or needs a rigid box

Shipping charges may be calculated using actual weight, volumetric weight or whichever is higher. A lightweight but large package can therefore cost more than expected. For example, cushions, gift hampers and some apparel packages occupy more space relative to their actual weight.

Ask each provider for the applicable volumetric formula and divisor. Do not assume that the formula is identical across carriers or plans. Also ask whether packaging material, pickup fees, remote-area charges, fuel surcharges or handling fees are billed separately.

### Customer locations

List the pincodes where your orders usually go. A provider can show impressive national coverage but still have weak delivery performance in the regions that matter to your business.

Check serviceability for:

- Metro cities
- Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities
- North-eastern states
- Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh and island territories
- Rural pincodes
- Industrial areas and large housing societies
- Locations where COD is frequently requested

For a Maharashtra business, do not evaluate only deliveries to Mumbai, Pune, Nashik and Nagpur. Test pincodes outside major urban centres if your customer base is statewide or national.

### Order pattern

The number and timing of orders matter. A small business with a few orders each day needs simple processing and responsive support. A growing brand may need automated order imports, multiple pickup locations and exception reporting.

Consider:

- Orders per day and per month
- Peak-season volume
- Weekend order flow
- Same-day dispatch capacity
- Number of warehouses
- Marketplace and website order mix
- Percentage of prepaid and COD orders
- Return and exchange frequency

Tell providers about expected peaks such as Diwali, regional festivals, end-of-season sales and campaign periods. Ask how pickup capacity is managed during those periods instead of assuming that normal service will continue unchanged.

### Customer promise

Decide what you want to promise customers before choosing a delivery service. You may offer standard delivery across India, faster delivery in selected cities or local delivery in Pune and nearby areas.

Do not publish a delivery promise based only on a courier’s general estimate. Your actual timeline also depends on order processing, packing, pickup cut-off, line-haul movement, local delivery and exceptions such as weather or address issues.

## Compare Logistics Models

In India, an online seller generally chooses between direct courier contracts, a shipping aggregator, a third-party logistics provider or a full D2C fulfilment service. Some companies combine these options.

### Direct courier account

You can contract directly with one or more courier companies. This may provide a dedicated commercial relationship and access to that carrier’s operational network.

The disadvantage is limited flexibility if a carrier does not serve a particular pincode well. You may also need to manage multiple dashboards, contracts, billing formats and support contacts if you use more than one courier.

Direct contracts are worth considering when your order volume is stable, your destinations are predictable and you have the operational capacity to manage carrier performance.

### Shipping aggregator

A shipping aggregator connects your store to multiple courier companies through one platform. It may offer rate comparisons, label generation, tracking, COD tools, return workflows and order synchronisation.

This model is useful for small and mid-sized businesses that want to start shipping without negotiating separate systems with every courier. It can also help route orders based on pincode, weight, service type or historical performance.

However, the lowest displayed rate may not be the final cost. Read the rate card and billing terms carefully. Verify whether the quoted rate includes GST, fuel surcharge, remote-area fees, COD charges, RTO charges, packaging and other adjustments.

### Third-party logistics provider

A 3PL may provide storage, inventory control, order processing, packing, dispatch and returns. This is different from using a shipping platform alone.

A 3PL can be useful when founders or internal staff are spending substantial time on packing and dispatch. It may also support multiple sales channels from a common inventory location.

The trade-off is greater operational dependence. You need clear rules for inventory receiving, stock counts, damaged goods, quality checks, order cut-offs, packaging standards and exit from the warehouse.

### D2C fulfilment service

D2C fulfilment is a broader service designed around online brands. It may include warehousing, pick-and-pack, shipping, returns, exchanges, COD reconciliation and integrations with platforms such as Shopify, WooCommerce or marketplaces.

It can be suitable for a brand with repeatable products and regular order volume. It may be less suitable for products requiring highly customised packing, frequent inspection or founder-level personalisation unless the provider supports those processes.

### Model comparison

| Model | Best suited for | Main advantages | Watch-outs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Direct courier account | Stable volume and predictable destinations | Direct relationship and carrier-specific operations | Less flexibility, separate systems and support |
| Shipping aggregator | Small and growing online sellers | Multiple carriers, one dashboard and easier setup | Rate-card complexity and dependence on platform support |
| 3PL warehouse | Businesses needing storage and dispatch help | Reduced internal packing work and centralised operations | Storage, handling, inventory and contract charges |
| D2C fulfilment | Brands with regular multi-channel orders | Integrated storage, packing, shipping and returns | Minimum commitments and less control over customised processes |
| Local delivery partner | Same-city or nearby delivery | Useful for urgent local orders and scheduled delivery | Limited geographic coverage and operational consistency |

There is no universally best model. Some brands use an aggregator for national courier shipments, a local delivery partner for Pune orders and a separate warehouse for high-volume products.

## Understand Shipping Rates and Total Cost

Shipping rates are important, but the quoted freight charge is only one part of logistics cost. Compare the complete landed cost per shipment.

### Components to check

Ask for a written rate card covering:

- Base freight
- GST
- COD fee or percentage
- Reverse pickup charge
- RTO freight
- Reattempt charges
- Volumetric weight rules
- Remote-area surcharge
- Fuel or seasonal surcharge
- Address correction charge
- NDR handling charge
- Packaging and consumables
- Warehouse receiving and storage
- Pick-and-pack fees
- Inventory transfer fees
- Cancellation charges
- Insurance or declared-value terms

A rate card should explain how slabs are applied. Ask whether weight is rounded up to the next slab and whether the original or final measured weight is used during billing. Also ask how disputes are raised and how long you have to challenge an incorrect weight or surcharge.

### Calculate cost by order type

Instead of comparing one sample shipment, create several scenarios:

1. Prepaid parcel to a metro city
2. COD parcel to a Tier 2 city
3. Lightweight but large package
4. Heavy parcel
5. Remote-area delivery
6. Returned prepaid order
7. Returned COD order
8. Exchange requiring forward and reverse movement

For each scenario, calculate the total cost. A partner with a slightly higher forward rate may be cheaper overall if it has better delivery completion and lower RTO.

A simple internal calculation is:

**Total logistics cost per order = forward shipping + COD fee + packaging + fulfilment fee + expected return cost + applicable surcharges**

This does not need to be a perfect financial model. Its purpose is to prevent a decision based on the headline shipping rate alone.

### GST and invoicing

Confirm how GST is shown on invoices and whether the billing entity, GSTIN and place-of-supply details suit your accounting process. Your accountant can advise on input tax credit and treatment for your specific business structure.

Check whether the provider gives downloadable invoices, shipment-level reconciliation and monthly statements. If your business sells through marketplaces as well as its own website, keep logistics invoices organised by sales channel and warehouse.

## Evaluate Delivery Operations

The logistics partner represents your brand after an order leaves your warehouse. You need visibility into what is happening, not only a tracking link shown to the customer.

### Pickup reliability

Ask:

- What are the pickup days and cut-off times?
- Is pickup scheduled automatically?
- What happens if the pickup executive does not arrive?
- Is there a backup process for missed pickups?
- Can pickup happen from more than one location?
- Are there restrictions on daily pickup volume?
- How are parcels scanned and acknowledged?

A parcel should not remain marked as “ready to ship” when it is still at your premises. Confirm when shipment responsibility moves from your team to the carrier and what proof is available.

### Tracking quality

Good tracking should show meaningful movement, such as pickup scheduled, picked up, in transit, at destination hub, out for delivery and delivered. A system that displays only broad status updates may not help your team answer customer queries.

Check whether tracking can be shared through:

- Customer emails
- SMS or WhatsApp notifications
- Your website or order page
- Shopify, WooCommerce or other store systems
- Marketplace dashboards
- Internal reports

Avoid committing to customer-facing delivery dates that your system cannot update when there is a delay.

### NDR management

NDR means non-delivery report. It can happen because the customer is unavailable, the address is incomplete, the phone number is unreachable or the customer refuses the parcel.

Ask how the provider handles NDR:

- How quickly is the issue reported?
- Can your team contact the customer through the dashboard?
- Can the delivery be reattempted?
- Can the address or phone number be corrected?
- How many attempts are made?
- When is a parcel moved to RTO?
- Is there a charge for every reattempt?

A practical NDR workflow can reduce avoidable returns. Your team should contact the customer promptly, verify the address and confirm whether the customer still wants the parcel. Do this without pressuring customers or misrepresenting the delivery status.

### COD operations

COD can help customers who do not prefer online payment, but it also introduces reconciliation and return risk.

Confirm:

- COD remittance schedule
- Settlement reports
- Bank account requirements
- Deduction details
- Failed remittance process
- Treatment of refused COD parcels
- Whether COD is available for all serviceable pincodes
- Whether cash collection is recorded at delivery

Match the provider’s settlement report with your order and bank records. Do not treat a parcel as financially complete merely because the dashboard shows “delivered”. Confirm that the collected amount has been accounted for.

## Examine RTO and Returns Before Signing

RTO, or return to origin, occurs when a shipment is not delivered and comes back to the sender. It may result from customer refusal, unreachable contact details, incomplete addresses, repeated delivery failure or operational problems.

RTO is especially important for COD-heavy categories and low-margin products. You may pay for forward movement, return movement, packaging, handling and lost selling time. The exact charges depend on the contract and carrier.

### Questions about RTO

Ask the provider:

- What events trigger RTO?
- How many delivery attempts are normally made?
- Are RTO charges the same as forward charges?
- Is an RTO parcel returned to the original warehouse?
- How quickly are RTO parcels received?
- Are damaged or opened returns documented?
- Can customers cancel before RTO?
- Is there an inspection or quality-check service?
- Can exchanges be processed instead of refunds?

Get the RTO terms in writing. Do not rely on a sales representative’s verbal explanation if the commercial agreement says something different.

### Build a returns process

Your returns policy should explain eligibility, time limits, product condition, refund method and exchange rules. The logistics provider can support the movement of the parcel, but your business remains responsible for communicating the policy accurately.

For returned goods, define:

- Who approves a return
- How the return label is created
- Which items cannot be returned
- How the parcel is inspected
- What happens if the item is damaged
- When the customer receives a refund
- How inventory is restocked
- How rejected returns are handled

If you sell cosmetics, food, medical products or intimate apparel, product-specific return rules may apply. Review your customer policy and fulfilment process with appropriate professional advice where required.

## Check Technology and Integrations

Technology should reduce manual work, not create another complicated process. Ask for a demonstration using your actual order flow.

### Essential integrations

Depending on your business, you may need integration with:

- Shopify
- WooCommerce
- Custom websites
- Amazon, Flipkart or other marketplaces
- Social commerce channels
- Inventory or ERP software
- Payment gateways
- Accounting systems
- WhatsApp or customer support tools

Check whether orders sync automatically, inventory is updated correctly and tracking is pushed back to the store. Ask what happens when an order is edited, cancelled, split or partially fulfilled.

### Access and data

Confirm user roles for founders, warehouse workers, customer support staff and accountants. Not every user should be able to change rates, cancel shipments or export all customer data.

Review:

- Data export options
- API availability
- Backup and downtime process
- Login security
- Audit trails
- Customer data retention
- Vendor access to personal information
- Process for closing the account

Logistics systems handle names, addresses, phone numbers and order details. Your agreements and internal practices should reflect applicable Indian privacy and data-protection requirements. Do not provide more customer information than the partner needs to perform delivery.

### Reports that matter

Useful reports may include:

- Orders by status
- Delivered and delayed shipments
- NDR ageing
- RTO by reason
- COD remittance
- Courier-wise performance
- Pincode-wise delivery issues
- Freight billed versus expected
- Weight discrepancies
- Return and exchange status

A dashboard is useful only if someone reviews it and acts on exceptions. Assign responsibility for checking delayed orders, open NDR cases and unpaid COD amounts.

## Assess Support, Contracts and Scalability

A logistics provider can have good software and still be difficult to work with when an order is stuck. Evaluate support before you need it.

### Support questions

Ask:

- Is support available by phone, email, ticket or WhatsApp?
- Is there a dedicated account manager?
- What is the escalation process?
- Who handles urgent delivery issues?
- How are lost or damaged parcels investigated?
- How are billing disputes resolved?
- Is support available during weekends and sale periods?

During the evaluation, raise a realistic sample issue. Observe whether the response is specific and actionable or merely a generic status update.

### Contract terms

Read the agreement for:

- Minimum shipment commitments
- Lock-in period
- Notice period
- Rate revision rights
- Payment terms
- Security deposit, if any
- Liability for loss and damage
- Claims procedure
- Service exclusions
- Suspension rights
- Data handling
- Account closure and data export

Avoid accepting a long commitment before testing the workflow. A pilot with selected pincodes and products can reveal problems that are not visible in a presentation.

### Scaling without disruption

Ask how the provider handles growth from a small daily order volume to a larger one. You do not need a promise of a particular delivery performance. You need to understand capacity, onboarding and operational controls.

Discuss:

- Additional pickup locations
- Multiple warehouses
- Bulk manifesting
- Seasonal volume
- Marketplace expansion
- New product categories
- Faster delivery options
- Regional fulfilment
- Inventory transfers
- Dedicated support at higher volume

A partner should make it possible to change the operating model when your business grows. At the same time, do not pay for complex fulfilment features before you need them.

## Use a Practical Evaluation Scorecard

Create a scorecard before taking vendor demonstrations. Score each shortlisted provider using your business priorities, not a generic template.

A possible structure is:

| Area | Questions to score |
|---|---|
| Coverage | Does the provider serve your important pincodes and product category? |
| Price | Is the total cost clear after GST, COD, RTO and other charges? |
| Delivery operations | Are pickup, tracking, NDR and escalation processes practical? |
| Returns | Can returns, exchanges and inspections be managed properly? |
| Technology | Do the required store, marketplace and inventory integrations work? |
| COD | Are settlement reports clear and remittances suitable for your cash flow? |
| Support | Can a real person resolve urgent shipment and billing issues? |
| Contract | Are liability, notice, rate changes and data terms acceptable? |
| Scalability | Can the provider support additional warehouses and higher volume? |
| Product fit | Does the provider understand your category’s packaging and handling needs? |

Give higher importance to the areas that affect your business most. For a fashion brand, exchanges and reverse logistics may matter more than the lowest forward rate. For a high-value electronics seller, security, proof of delivery and claims handling may be more important.

### Run a controlled pilot

Start with a limited pilot rather than moving every order immediately. Use a mix of:

- Prepaid and COD orders
- Metro and non-metro destinations
- Small and large packages
- New and repeat customers
- Standard and return shipments

Track actual charges against quoted rates. Note how quickly support responds, whether tracking updates are accurate and whether COD reports match your own records.

The pilot should answer practical questions:

- Were pickups completed as scheduled?
- Were labels and invoices correct?
- Did the system sync orders properly?
- Were customers able to track shipments?
- Were NDR cases visible?
- Were RTO reasons understandable?
- Did billing contain unexpected adjustments?
- Did returned items arrive in acceptable condition?

Only after reviewing these results should you decide whether to expand the arrangement.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

### Choosing only on the lowest rate

A low forward rate can be offset by expensive RTO, COD, remote-area or weight-dispute charges. Compare the complete cost for your actual order mix.

### Ignoring packaging

Poor packaging increases damage, leakage and customer complaints. Ask whether the provider supplies packaging, follows your packing instructions and records damage at handover or return.

### Using one carrier for every pincode

No single carrier is necessarily strongest in every region or product category. A multi-carrier arrangement may offer better resilience, provided your team can manage the system.

### Not checking COD reconciliation

COD money affects working capital. Set a process for matching delivered orders, expected remittances and bank credits.

### Treating all RTO as the customer’s fault

Some RTOs happen because of incorrect addresses or customer unavailability. Others may involve delayed movement, inadequate attempts or operational errors. Review reason codes before changing your customer policy.

### Moving to fulfilment too early

A fulfilment warehouse can save time, but storage and handling charges may not make sense for low or unpredictable order volume. First calculate the internal cost of packing and dispatching yourself.

### Failing to plan for exit

Keep your own product, order, customer and accounting records. Understand how open shipments, inventory, returns and data will be handled if you change providers.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the difference between a courier company and a logistics aggregator?

A courier company carries parcels through its own delivery network or operating arrangements. A logistics aggregator connects sellers to multiple courier companies through one technology and billing layer. An aggregator may offer routing, tracking and COD tools, but the exact service depends on the carriers available through its platform.

### Is COD still important for Indian e-commerce businesses?

COD may remain relevant for customers who do not prefer online payment or have concerns about prepaid orders. Its suitability depends on your product category, customer locations, margins and RTO experience. Compare COD conversion with the cost of failed deliveries and cash reconciliation before expanding COD availability.

### How can an online seller reduce RTO?

Use accurate addresses and phone numbers, send clear order confirmations, provide tracking updates and contact customers promptly when an NDR is raised. You can also test prepaid incentives or partial payment, but any change should be explained clearly to customers. Review RTO reasons by pincode, courier and product instead of applying one rule to every order.

### Should a small D2C brand use a 3PL warehouse?

A 3PL may make sense when storage, packing and dispatch are taking significant internal time or when orders come from multiple channels. It may not be economical for very low, irregular or highly customised order volumes. Compare warehouse, receiving, pick-and-pack, packaging, shipping and return charges with your current internal cost.

### How do I compare shipping rates correctly?

Use the same package weights, dimensions, destinations and service type for every provider. Include GST, COD, RTO, reverse pickup, remote-area, fuel, packaging and other applicable charges. Compare several order scenarios rather than relying on one metro prepaid shipment.

### What should I do if a logistics provider loses or damages a parcel?

Keep the order invoice, packing evidence, handover scan, shipment photographs where appropriate and customer communication. Raise the claim within the provider’s stated time limit and follow the contract’s documentation process. For high-value products, confirm liability and insurance terms before shipping rather than after a loss.

## Where to Start

Prepare a one-page shipping brief with your products, package dimensions, average and peak order volume, important pincodes, prepaid-to-COD mix, return process and required integrations. Shortlist providers that support your product and customer locations, then request complete rate cards and contract terms.

Run a controlled pilot and record actual freight, COD, RTO, support and reconciliation outcomes. Choose the logistics partner that provides a workable total cost and dependable operational visibility, not merely the most attractive introductory shipping rate.
